notes.key_messages: • In calculations, candidates must set out and explain their working correctly. When candidates give an incorrect final answer and no working is shown, it is impossible for any partial credit to be awarded for those parts that are correct. • Candidates sometimes needed to be clearer and more precise when answering questions requiring a description or explanation. • It is important that candidates read the questions carefully in order to understand exactly what is being asked. • In order to improve their performance, candidates should practice applying their knowledge to new situations by attempting questions in support materials or exam papers from previous sessions.
notes.general_comments: Many candidates were well prepared for this paper. Equations were generally well known by stronger candidates but a significant number of other candidates struggled to even recall them. Often candidates knew how to apply their knowledge and understanding to fairly standard situations. On occasions, when asked to apply their knowledge to a new situation, they displayed a lack of breadth of understanding. More successful candidates were willing to think through the possibilities and apply their knowledge when the question asked for suggestions to explain new situations. Less successful candidates had difficulty in applying their knowledge to new situations and did not show the stages in their working. The English language ability of the majority of the candidates was adequate for the demands of this paper. A very small number of candidates struggled to express themselves adequately. In some cases, numbers were not legibly written which was problematic. The topic of total internal reflection was poorly understood by the vast majority of candidates, as was the reason for placing the switch in the live wire of a mains circuit.
notes.1ai: The majority of candidates answered fully correctly. Common errors were to forget to subtract 1.5, or to ignore the ruler in the diagram and take measurements directly from the paper.
notes.1aii: Most candidates were able to gain at least partial credit on this question.
notes.1b: Most candidates recalled the equation for density and successfully evaluated the density as 7.8 g / cm .
notes.2a: Most candidates identified regions ST or WX for constant speed, XY for constant deceleration, and TW for constant acceleration. Despite being asked for a constant speed when the cyclist was moving, a significant number chose region YZ.
notes.2b: Almost all candidates recalled that distance travelled was equal to the area under the speed–time graph and went on to calculate the distance travelled as 120 m. A common error was to halve this distance or to calculate the total distance travelled by the cyclist.
notes.2ci: The majority of candidates correctly calculated the resultant force as 60 N. The most common error was to add the two forces rather than subtract.
notes.2cii: Only stronger candidates recognised that the resultant force would cause the cyclist to accelerate. A common error was simply to state that the cyclist would move forward.
notes.3a: Many candidates struggled to identify the correct energy store or means of energy transfer in this question.
notes.3b: Most candidates recalled the equation for work done and evaluated this as 6.8 J. A common error was to divide the quantities rather than multiply.
notes.3c: The majority of candidates recalled the equation for pressure, and correctly evaluated this as 0.19 N / cm . A common error was to invert the quantities and divide 44 by 8.5.
notes.4ai: Many candidates gained full credit for this question.
notes.4aii: Only stronger candidates answered this correctly. Other candidates were unable to link the decrease in temperature to a decrease in kinetic energy of particles.
notes.4bi: This new section on the syllabus was only understood by stronger candidates. Very few recalled that the temperature at which particles have least kinetic energy is called absolute zero.
notes.4bii: The vast majority of candidates thought that absolute zero was 0 °C.
notes.4c: Candidates found this question challenging. Most thought that a good emitter would have a shiny white surface.
notes.5ai: Most candidates correctly calculated the distance as 612 m. A common error was to divide 340 by 1.8 instead of multiplying.
notes.5aii: The majority of candidates recognised that the sound was caused by sound waves reflecting but did not state that they had reflected from a rocky surface. Weaker candidates thought that sound waves reflected off each other.
notes.5b: Most candidates correctly calculated the frequency as 1200 Hz. However, many candidates used an incorrect rearrangement of the equation, and failed to gain any credit. Candidates should be encouraged to write down the standard arrangement of the equation before they attempt any rearrangement.
notes.6ai: Many candidates recognised the process as refraction. Common errors included diffraction, reflection and even some rarefactions.
notes.6aii: The majority of candidates recognised that the speed, wavelength and direction of travel of the wave had changed. Weaker candidates just stated that the wavefronts were bent, which was insufficient for credit.
notes.6b: The topic of total internal reflection was not well understood by most candidates. Stronger candidates sometimes gained partial credit.
notes.7ai: The concept of induced magnetism was not well understood by most candidates. Only the strongest candidates stated that the magnetised nail would have the opposite pole in contact with the pole of the magnet.
notes.7aii: Many candidates were able to give a difference in the magnetic properties of iron and steel. However, many candidates interchanged the properties of iron and steel.
notes.7bi: Only stronger candidates stated that when the wire was stationary, the reading on the voltmeter was zero volts.
notes.7bii: The concept of electromagnetic induction was not well understood by most candidates. Very few stated that the wire would cut the magnetic field lines of the magnet when it moved.
notes.8a: Candidates found this question challenging and a significant number did not give an answer. Many who attempted the question interchanged the positions of the ammeter and voltmeter.
notes.8b: Many candidates correctly calculated the resistance of the heater as 5.7 ohms. However, a very common error was to multiply 8 by 1.4 instead of dividing.
notes.8c: Many candidates correctly calculated the energy from the heater as 336 J, but the vast majority could not recall or use the equation E = V I t . Candidates should be encouraged to learn the new equations on in the syllabus and to practice using them in examples.
notes.9a: Candidates found this question challenging. Very few recalled that the switch is fitted into the live wire and an even smaller number could explain the reasons for this.
notes.9bi: The majority of candidates recognised the transformer as a step-down transformer.
notes.9bii: Very few candidates recalled the structure of a step-down transformer. Only the strongest candidates gained full credit.
notes.10ai: The majority of candidates correctly stated that the number of protons was 53.
notes.10aii: Fewer candidates were able to determine the number of neutrons as 78.
notes.10b: Candidates found this question challenging. Very few recalled that a beta-particle was an electron and that a gamma ray is an electromagnetic wave.
notes.10c: Many candidates correctly calculated the mass of iodine. However, other candidates did not gain any credit for this question. Candidates should be encouraged to clearly state the number of half- lives involved in calculations such as this and then to clearly set out their working using this number of half-lives.
notes.11a: Many candidates found this question challenging.
notes.11b: Very few candidates gave a detailed description of planetary formation using the accretion model from the syllabus. A significant number described the life cycle of a star.
